title: Indicator Removal: Relocate Malware
summary: Relocate Malware is the copying of a payload to new paths on the same host, or to further hosts, followed by cleanup of the original, so that the file an analyst first identified stops existing and the surviving copy has no obvious history. Attackers rename each copy to match the legitimate contents of the destination folder, place it in a location that security products exclude from scanning or that a known persistence mechanism already uses, and then delete the earlier artefacts. The evasive value comes from how file metadata behaves: a copy or a move on the same volume usually keeps the original creation time, so detection logic that waits for newly created files in sensitive directories sees nothing, and the link between the initial delivery event and the later execution is broken across paths and process records. Cloud and remote cases look similar, where a copy is staged on one instance or host before it is used further. Because relocation is not an attack in itself, detection leans on provenance rather than on the file. Endpoint telemetry that records copies and renames, command lines that combine a copy with a delete, file writes into excluded or unusual directories, the same payload hash or imphash appearing under a new name, and process trees that reach a document, download, or share immediately before the write are the practical pivots, and each copy should be treated as a separate artefact with its own timestamps and security descriptor to compare.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker makes copies of their own malware in new places and then removes the original file. The copies are often given names that fit the folder they sit in. The aim is to hide the payload and to confuse investigators.
beginner.whyItMatters: When a security tool reports a malicious file, you expect to find that file. If it has been copied elsewhere and the original deleted, your search for the file fails. Your picture of the attack also breaks, because you lose the link between the first infection and later actions.
howItWorks: A payload arrives on a computer, for example through a document, a download, or a shared folder.
The attacker copies that file to one or more new locations using built-in file commands.
They rename each copy so it matches the normal file names already in that folder.
They choose folders that security tools are told to skip, or folders that another program already uses.
Copying the file usually keeps its original creation time, so it does not look newly created.
Finally they delete the original file and any earlier copies, which hides where the attack started.
beginner.example: A thief hides a stolen parcel in a left luggage office. Instead of keeping it in one locker, they move it into several lockers under different labels, each label matching the other luggage there. Then they empty the first locker and throw away the label.
takeaways: Relocating malware is defence evasion, and it breaks the link between an alert and the first infection.
Copies often keep the old creation time, so a new file time is not a reliable signal.
Track a payload by content, such as its hash, rather than by its file name or its path.

objectives: Explain why attackers copy and rename a payload after it has been delivered.
Describe how copying a file affects its recorded times and why that matters.
Identify directories that attackers target, such as scanner exclusions and persistence paths.
Describe which endpoint telemetry records file copies, moves, and renames.
Explain how hashes and process ancestry connect a moved payload to its origin.
